summary: This work demonstrates a unified flux control architecture for fluxonium qubits that consolidates both transverse ($XY$) and longitudinal ($Z$) operations into a single flux-control channel, reducing hardware overhead compared to conventional multi-channel approaches. High-fidelity operation is achieved through frequency-selective cryogenic filtering combined with compensated waveform synthesis and instruction-level FPGA-native synthesis.
motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors requires reducing control hardware complexity while maintaining performance. Fluxonium qubits enable single-channel universal control via their fluxon-tunneling-based transitions at hundreds of MHz, unlike transmons at few GHz, but require reconciling competing demands: low-frequency transmission for reset operations, broadband noise suppression for coherence, and accurate microwave delivery for high-fidelity gates.
method: A Gaussian low-pass filter with 92 MHz cutoff at the 4 K stage, combined with 30 dB cryogenic attenuation, suppresses room-temperature broadband noise while preserving coherence. Pulse distortion from the filtered control line is corrected via bounded inverse-filter pre-distortion ($H_\mathrm{inv}(f) = H_\mathrm{qubit}/\max[H_\mathrm{gauss}(f), 10^{-G_\mathrm{max}/20}] \times W(f)$ with $G_\mathrm{max} = 50$ dB). Instruction-level waveform synthesis on FPGA uses 5-tap IIR filtering for the $Z$ path and 16-tap FIR filtering for $XY$ modulation, enabling dynamic pulse generation from reusable primitives rather than stored waveforms.
result: Device A maintains $T_1 = 110$ µs, $T_2^R = 128$ µs, $T_2^\mathrm{echo} = 133$ µs; achieves active reset with $\sim$98% fidelity and $\Delta\Phi_\mathrm{dc} \approx 0.298\,\Phi_0$ excursion; single-qubit gates with 20 ns duration exceed 99.99% fidelity via randomized benchmarking. Across seven additional devices (208–378 MHz), fidelities reach 99.97% or higher for frequencies below 300 MHz; at 378 MHz with 200 ns gates, coherence times exceed 100 µs, confirming scalability of the architecture.
